acts.title: Text A · Why a man would post himself
text: By the time Henry Brown climbed into the crate, he had already lost everything the law allowed him to have.

He had been born into slavery in Virginia in 1816, and from the age of fifteen he had worked in a tobacco factory. His owner had treated him less brutally than most: Brown was paid something for his work, and he had never suffered physical abuse. That was the whole of his good fortune.

In 1836 he had married a woman named Nancy, whose owner had promised not to sell her. They had three children and were expecting a fourth when the promise was broken. Nancy and the children were sold to a man in North Carolina.
Brown asked his own owner for help and was told he could get another wife. The next morning he walked four miles holding Nancy’s hand, until the wagons took her away. He never saw any of them again.

items.q: What was unusual about Brown’s situation before the escape?
o: He was paid for his work and had not been physically abused

items.q: What made him decide to escape?
o: His wife and children were sold away from him
He was moved to another state

acts.title: Text B · Twenty-seven hours in a box
text: The plan was simple enough to sound impossible. Brown had asked a friend who was a carpenter to build a crate three feet long, two and a half deep and two wide. Two other friends had already contacted an anti-slavery organization in Philadelphia, which had agreed to receive the package.
He painted “right side up with care” on the outside, took some water, and got in.

By the time the crate reached Philadelphia it had travelled on three trains, two boats and three road wagons. The instruction on the lid had been ignored for most of the journey. At one point Brown had been sitting upside down for several hours and came close to dying.
When the lid finally came off, the men who had been waiting all morning were too tense to speak. Brown stood up, disorientated and alive, and said good morning.

items.s: A carpenter friend built the crate to Brown’s measurements.
Nobody in Philadelphia knew the crate was coming.
The instruction painted on the lid was followed carefully throughout.
Brown spent several hours upside down and nearly died.
The men waiting were relaxed while they waited.
Brown was alive when the crate was opened.

What is the form of the past perfect?
“He had been sitting upside down for several hours.” What does the continuous add?
o: How long it had gone on

items.q: Why is the past perfect needed in these sentences at all?
o: The story is already in the past, and these events are earlier still

acts.title: The past perfect: a past inside a past
rule: A story sits at some moment in the past. The past perfect is what you use for anything that happened before that moment. It is not “a more past tense” — it is a way of telling the reader that you have stepped backwards, and that you are about to step forward again.
points: had + past participle, for every subject. He had gone, they had gone.
had been + -ing, when the duration matters. He had been sitting for hours.
Only when the order would otherwise be unclear. After after, before and then, the past simple is often enough, because the order is already obvious.
by the time, already, never, just, and superlatives with ever.
eg: By the time he climbed in, he had already lost everything.
The loss came first.
He had been born into slavery in 1816.
A step back from the story’s present.
The friends had already contacted the organization.
already — a favourite with the past perfect.
It was the first time he had travelled by boat.
First time + past perfect.
It was the most frightening thing he had ever done.
Superlative + ever.
He had been sitting upside down for several hours.
Continuous — the duration is the point.
The men who had been waiting all morning were exhausted.
Continuous, describing why they were exhausted.
After he arrived, he became a member of the movement.
No past perfect needed: after makes the order clear.
She had never seen a gorilla before that morning.
never + before.
I did not recognize him. He had grown a beard.
The second sentence explains the first by stepping back.
acts.careful: Do not put the whole story into the past perfect. Once you have stepped back and explained, step forward again into the past simple, or the reader loses the thread.

acts.title: Two events, one order, three sentences
steps: He lost his family. Later, he climbed into the crate.
Two events. In real time, the loss came first.
1 · Choose the moment your story sits at. That one stays in the PAST SIMPLE.
By the time he climbed into the crate…
2 · Signal the step backwards. by the time, when, before.
By the time he climbed into the crate, he had lost…
3 · Put the EARLIER event into the past perfect: had + past participle.
By the time he climbed into the crate, he had already lost his family.
4 · Add already if the point is that it was complete.

Which part of the pair stays in the past simple?
o: The later event — the moment the story sits at

write.q: Write about 180 words telling the story of something that happened to you or to somebody you know, where part of the explanation lies further back in time. Use the past perfect at least four times and the past perfect continuous at least once, but keep the main events in the past simple.
plan: the moment the story sits at
what had already happened before it
write.model:
By the time my grandfather reached Karaganda in 1953, he had already been travelling for eleven days, and he had lost the only photograph he owned.

He had grown up in a village near Rostov and had trained as a mechanic there, which was the only reason he was allowed on the transport at all. He had never been further east than the river.

The events themselves are dull, which is what people always leave out. He arrived, he was assigned a bed in a hut with fourteen other men, and he started work on a Tuesday. He stayed for forty-one years.

What he talked about, when he talked about it, was the photograph. He had been carrying it inside his coat for the whole journey, and somewhere between two trains it went. He never told us who was in it.

It was the first time he had lived anywhere without family, and I think he decided quite early that it would also be the last.
